rawInput.complaint:
A 20-year-old woman was referred for constant right proximal thigh pain that had progressed over 8 years. She had no other medical conditions, menarche at age 13, and no family history of bone disease. The pain was worse at night, somewhat relieved by activity and cold baths, and required daily NSAIDs, paracetamol, and weak opioids. She had a leg-length discrepancy managed with shoe inserts and was on sick leave due to her symptoms. At age 11 she had hip joint pain with an ultrasound-guided aspiration revealing sterile fluid; pain resolved. Six months prior, she was hit by a car at knee level, with no fracture diagnosed, after which her thigh pain worsened.

On examination, there were no skin lesions, café au lait spots, erythema, heat, or swelling over the right thigh. Leg lengths were slightly unequal but within normal limits.

Magnetic resonance imaging and PET–CT showed significant increased cortical thickness of the right femoral diaphysis with partial medullary obliteration and an uneven sclerotic surface. A Tc-99m bone scan demonstrated increased uptake in most of the right femoral shaft. Biochemical bone markers, including alkaline phosphatase, were normal. Genetic screening in blood for the GNAS1 R201 mutation and for SQSTM1 mutations was negative. Bone biopsy of the lesion revealed thickened bone trabeculae with preserved lamellar structure, accentuated cement lines, and no fibrosis, inflammation, alcian positivity, malignancy, or neoplasia.

cotDiagnosis.reasoning:
The chief complaint is chronic, progressive right proximal thigh pain in a 20-year-old woman, present for 8 years and severe enough to require daily analgesics and cause sick leave. The patient’s main concern is persistent unilateral femoral pain that is worse at night and has worsened further after minor trauma, without evidence of fracture.

Salient positive findings are the very long duration, unilateral localization to the right femur, and imaging showing a structural bone process rather than soft-tissue disease: MRI and PET-CT demonstrated marked cortical thickening of the right femoral diaphysis, partial obliteration of the medullary canal, and an uneven sclerotic surface; bone scan showed increased uptake in most of the right femoral shaft, indicating active bone turnover in that segment. She also had a mild leg-length discrepancy and prior childhood hip pain on the same side. Histology is especially important: thickened trabeculae with preserved lamellar structure and accentuated cement lines, without fibrosis, inflammation, alcian positivity, malignancy, or neoplasia. Bone markers including alkaline phosphatase were normal.

Pertinent negatives help narrow the diagnosis. There were no café-au-lait spots or skin lesions, arguing against syndromic McCune-Albright syndrome. There was no erythema, heat, or swelling, and biopsy showed no inflammation, making chronic osteomyelitis unlikely. There was no malignancy or neoplasia on biopsy, arguing against osteosarcoma or other primary bone tumor. The lesion is extensive along most of the femoral shaft rather than a small nidus, which argues against osteoid osteoma despite nocturnal pain and NSAID responsiveness. SQSTM1 testing was negative and the patient is very young, making Paget disease less likely, though histologic cement lines can overlap.

The main candidate differentials are fibrous dysplasia, Paget disease of bone, chronic sclerosing osteomyelitis, and osteoid osteoma/osteoblastoma.

Fibrous dysplasia fits several core features best: onset in childhood/adolescence, monostotic involvement of a single long bone, pain, mild limb asymmetry/leg-length discrepancy, and imaging showing expansion/sclerosis of the femur. Although classic fibrous dysplasia often shows fibro-osseous tissue histologically, this biopsy instead showed dense lamellar bone with accentuated cement lines and no fibrosis. However, this pattern is compatible with the sclerotic “pagetoid” variant of fibrous dysplasia described in monostotic lesions, especially in the proximal femur. The absence of GNAS1 mutation in blood does not exclude fibrous dysplasia because the mutation is somatic and mosaic, often absent in peripheral blood.

Paget disease is a consideration because of cortical thickening, medullary narrowing, increased uptake on bone scan, and accentuated cement lines on histology. However, it is much less likely in a 20-year-old, alkaline phosphatase was normal, SQSTM1 testing was negative, and the clinical context is childhood onset with a solitary femoral lesion rather than typical adult-onset Paget disease.

Chronic sclerosing osteomyelitis could cause pain and sclerosis, but there are no systemic or local inflammatory signs, no biopsy evidence of inflammation, and no mention of infectious features. Osteoid osteoma is less likely because the lesion involves most of the femoral shaft with diffuse cortical thickening and medullary obliteration rather than a focal nidus.

Overall, the diagnosis that best integrates the age at onset, monostotic unilateral femoral involvement, chronic pain, leg-length discrepancy, imaging pattern, and exclusion of infection and malignancy is monostotic fibrous dysplasia of the femur, specifically a sclerotic/pagetoid variant.

differentialDiagnoses.supportingEvidence: Childhood/adolescent onset, solitary right femoral involvement, chronic pain, mild leg-length discrepancy, bone scan uptake in the affected shaft, and biopsy excluding malignancy/inflammation; blood GNAS1 negativity does not exclude mosaic fibrous dysplasia.

Cortical thickening, partial medullary obliteration, increased uptake, and accentuated cement lines could resemble Paget disease, but age 20, normal alkaline phosphatase, and negative SQSTM1 make it less likely.
Can produce painful sclerotic long-bone lesions, but there were no inflammatory signs clinically and biopsy showed no inflammation.
Night pain and NSAID response are suggestive, but imaging showed diffuse involvement of most of the femoral shaft without a focal nidus, and biopsy did not show a bone-forming tumor.

cotDiagnosis.finalDiagnosis: Monostotic fibrous dysplasia of the right femur
